faqs.q: Why does an Ashland chimney raccoon job cost more than a simple attic removal?
faqs.a: A flue is specialized work. The crew has to confirm whether young are down the chimney, remove the family without anyone — animal or human — getting hurt, clean out nesting debris, and fit a cap sized to a historic flue that may be oversized or unlined. Attic-only jobs skip the flue work entirely. After inspecting your chimney and roofline we quote the whole sequence in writing, cap included, so there is no second bill for finishing the job properly.

faqs.q: There are birds swooping out of my Ashland chimney all summer — can they be removed?
faqs.a: If they are chimney swifts — slim, sooty birds that cling inside the flue and chatter at dusk — they cannot. Swifts are federally protected native birds, they are excluded from what a Virginia nuisance permit covers, and an active nest with eggs or young stays until the young fledge in late summer. The good news is that swifts eat insects, damage nothing, and leave on their own; once they have gone we can clean the flue and fit screening that keeps next year's swifts — and this winter's raccoons — out, if you would rather host neither.

Ashland.wildlife_intro:
Ashland's trains built a town of tall houses and taller chimneys, and raccoons have been reading that skyline ever since. An uncapped Ashland flue is a hollow tree with better weather protection, so spring brings a steady run of raccoon mothers denning in chimneys from the historic center out to the college streets — with chimney swifts, a protected native bird, nesting in other flues all summer and off-limits until their young leave. Ashland's woods are never far away — Stony Run and Mechumps Creek thread the town edges — so sealing is only half the job. We cap the flue properly once the family is out, screen the vents swifts and squirrels both use, and check the whole roofline, because a raccoon turned away from one Ashland chimney usually tests two more on the same street before the week is out.

faqs.q: How is mole work in Elmont priced, and why not just a flat rate?
faqs.a: Because a mole job is measured in active tunnel systems, not in moles anyone can count. One Elmont yard may hold a single animal working a fresh ridge line; the next may have overlapping systems across an acre of soft bottomland soil, needing more traps and more check visits — Virginia law requires traps to be visited daily. We map the active runs during inspection, quote that mapped scope, and explain how grub treatment and watering habits affect whether new moles move in afterward.

faqs.q: Beavers keep flooding my Elmont field ditch — what are my real options?
faqs.a: Beaver are one of the few Virginia species a landowner may have removed when they are causing damage, and a permit holder can do that work — but on Chickahominy bottomland, removing beavers without addressing the dam site usually buys a quiet season, not a solution, because the habitat stays ideal. We talk through the honest menu: dam and beaver removal, water-level control devices where the ditch layout allows them, and tree protection for the plantings you care about — and which combination fits your ground, rather than selling the first option.

Elmont.wildlife_intro:
Elmont lives in the Chickahominy River's shadow — swamp forest and floodplain press against farm fields and subdivision fences, and the water table keeps the ground soft enough for eastern moles to ridge a lawn in a single wet week. Mole runs are Elmont's most common call, but the bottomland sends variety: beavers dam drainage ditches and flood field edges, northern watersnakes patrol the wet ditches (harmless, and forever being mistaken for something worse), and raccoons commute from the swamp woods into crawlspaces all winter.

Low, wet ground changes how jobs are done here. Mole work means reading fresh surface runs after rain rather than guessing at a dry yard, beaver conflicts mean water-control thinking instead of simple trapping talk, and crawlspace sealing has to account for the moisture that rots vents and sills in the first place. We tell Elmont homeowners plainly which problems we can solve outright and which ones the river will keep renegotiating.
